questions.q: Why do naming conventions matter more in a warehouse than in a typical OLTP schema?
options: A warehouse holds many fact and dimension tables, often queried directly by analysts who didn't design the schema and need to understand a table's role at a glance
SQL Server requires warehouse table names to follow a stricter character set than OLTP tables
Naming conventions only matter for security reasons
OLTP tables cannot have prefixes at all
questions.explain: Consistent naming lets someone unfamiliar with the schema immediately recognize a table's role and how to join it, without consulting a data dictionary first.

questions.q: What does the Fact_ / Dim_ table prefix convention communicate?
options: Whether a table is a fact table (measures at a grain) or a dimension table (descriptive attributes), at a glance
The physical filegroup the table is stored on
Whether the table has a clustered index
The exact number of rows in the table
questions.explain: An analyst who sees Fact_Sales immediately knows it's a fact table to aggregate and filter, while Dim_Product is a dimension to browse for descriptive attributes.

questions.q: Per this lesson's column-naming pattern, how should a surrogate key be named, and how should a natural/business key be named?
options: Surrogate keys end in Key (e.g. ProductKey); natural keys are named for their source instead (e.g. ProductAlternateKey), so nobody joins on the wrong one
Both should be named identically to avoid confusion
Surrogate keys should never have any suffix at all
Natural keys should always be named Key1, Key2, Key3, etc.
questions.explain: The visual distinction (Key suffix vs. a source-named column) prevents someone from accidentally joining fact tables on a natural key instead of the correct surrogate key.

questions.q: What does this lesson say about audit/lineage columns like LoadDateTime across multiple tables?
options: They should use a fixed, identically-spelled set of names on every table that has them, not different names like LoadedOn on one table and Load_Date on another
Every table should invent its own unique audit column names
Audit columns should never be included in a warehouse schema
Audit columns must always be the first column in the table
questions.explain: Using the exact same audit column names (LoadDateTime, SourceSystem, RowStartDate, RowEndDate, IsCurrent) everywhere makes the whole warehouse predictable to query.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what matters more than which specific naming convention a warehouse team picks?
options: Applying the chosen convention with zero exceptions across the whole warehouse
Using the absolute shortest possible table and column names
Matching the naming convention used by the source OLTP system exactly
Avoiding underscores in all object names
questions.explain: No specific convention (prefix vs. suffix, PascalCase vs. snake_case) is objectively correct — consistency across the entire warehouse is what actually matters.
